items.question: What do you find valuable about the speed of virtual agents’ meetings?
items.object: Virtual agents’ meetings
items.answer: One nice thing about these virtual agents is that their meetings are much faster than our meetings, right? In the time that we sit around and introduce each other and have coffee, they already had hundreds of meetings.

items.question: How do you see the potential for extracting new knowledge from existing protein language models?
items.object: Knowledge hidden in existing protein language models
items.answer: These protein language models, I think they have learned new concepts; they have filled in some of the gaps in our knowledge. Now it's our job to see: can we extract those out using techniques like SAEs? I do think that there is already a gold mine of new concepts and knowledge that are already hidden in the existing models. Even if we can extract those out, I think that would already teach us a huge amount of interesting new insights.

items.question: How do you think about Virtual Lab as a platform for tackling open-ended scientific research?
items.object: Virtual Lab
items.answer: I'm very excited about Virtual Lab. The setup there is that it's a very versatile platform, right? We have an AI professor, sort of like an AI professor agent, and that professor agent then manages and works with a bunch of different agents that you can view as student agents. Each of the sub-agents would have their own expertise. You can have one agent being an immunologist expert, a computer science expert, or a computational biology expert. The professor and this team of virtual agents work together to tackle these quite challenging, open-ended research projects. We did a case study of having this team, Virtual Lab, try to design new nanobodies for the recent variant of SARS-CoV-2.

items.question: What do you find exciting about the Virtual Lab agents’ work on designing new nanobodies?
items.object: Virtual Lab’s computational workflow for designing nanobodies
items.answer: I think the headline result is that this Virtual Lab of agents with diverse interdisciplinary expertise worked together and actually did something very cool, with relatively minimal human feedback from us. They first developed a new computational framework or workflow for designing new nanobodies. This computational platform that they developed uses quite sophisticated tools like protein language models like ESM; they use AlphaFold, they also use Rosetta and more physics-based tools. Each of the tools had been used before in previous studies, of course, but the way that the agents modified these tools and put them together into this overall pipeline is new, to the best of our knowledge. That's something that's already very cool. The part that's maybe even more exciting is that they actually used this new pipeline to develop a bunch of nanobodies.

items.question: Why do you see the binding profiles of the nanobodies you experimentally tested as particularly promising?
items.object: Experimentally tested nanobodies that bind across viral variants
items.answer: We actually then made those nanobodies and physically and experimentally tested them. A couple of these antibodies actually look very promising in terms of having strong binding profiles to some of the recent variants, while retaining and even improving binding profiles to some of the earlier variants. I think that's sort of like a holy grail, because you want to have potential vaccines or therapeutics that can bind well across a diversity of variants even as the viruses evolve over time.

items.question: How do you see Virtual Lab addressing the limitations of earlier approaches to AI agents for science?
items.object: Virtual Lab’s approach to human–AI scientific collaboration
items.answer: There's a lot of exciting progress in research projects trying to use agents for science. A lot of the previous works on agents for science, or language models for science more broadly, are looking at much narrower tasks: narrow in the sense that the human researchers would define, “Here's exactly what I want to do, and here are the different steps,” and then have the agents do the lower-level implementations and executions of those steps. The other mode is where the agents come up with research ideas, but then the agents really don't do very much of the actual execution, and certainly there's very little experimental validation, the real-world grounding of those research ideas. Virtual Lab is designed to address some of those limitations and be much more flexible. It's still a human-AI collaboration, but the human feedback to those AI agents in the Virtual Lab is relatively limited. We don't actually write the code for them or do the work, and we don't even tell them, “Here's exactly what you have to do, A, B, and C.” In this case, we, the human researchers, would tell the Virtual Lab, “Okay, we're interested in designing potentially new therapeutics or new vaccines for the recent variants of SARS-CoV-2.” From a high-level description, the agents actually have to decide first what approach they want to take, and then how they try to achieve that goal.

items.question: How do you see the Virtual Lab agents’ role in developing their own scientific tool workflow?
items.object: Virtual Lab agents’ role in selecting, modifying, and combining scientific tools
items.answer: These agents, they're GPT-4o under the hood, so they're aware of a lot of the popular, powerful tools in the literature. We don't actually tell them, “You have to use AlphaFold” or “You have to use ESM.” Through one of these Virtual Lab meetings, they decided, “Here's a list of potential tools.” Maybe they came up initially with a list of six or eight different tools, and subsequently they decided, “Here are the three tools that may be the most relevant”: ESM, AlphaFold multimer, and Rosetta, which have complementary strengths. They decided they actually wanted to modify some of the tools like ESM in ways that we haven't seen been done before in previous papers, and also put these different tools together into a new workflow. The parts from deciding what tools to use, modifying the tools, which I think is a critical component, and putting the different tools together into a pipeline are mostly done by the agents.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the agents’ modification of ESM’s protein-sequence scoring method?
items.object: The agents’ modification of ESM’s protein-sequence scoring method
items.answer: I think this is actually something quite interesting that agents developed. Just for the general audience, ESM is a large protein language model. You can think of it as a BERT-style model, but trained over amino acid sequences, and it's trained over all these evolutionary-scale sequences of proteins. You can give it a new protein sequence, or modify some protein sequence by introducing some mutations, and the ESM model will produce a basic log-likelihood score, similar to perplexity in large language models. That'll tell you how likely this modified sequence is. The general intuition is that if the modified sequence is stable, if it's actually a functional protein, then the log likelihood would be relatively good, a relatively high score. But there's actually a lot of fine art in how exactly to compute those log-likelihood scores and exactly which ones to use. The agent here actually developed a new formula for computing a specific way to think of this likelihood ratio score, which is different from previous publications where people had used ESM. That's actually an interesting local modification or innovation by the agents.

items.question: Why do you consider the AI agents’ formula for computing likelihood ratios during sequential nanobody mutations reasonable?
items.object: AI agents’ formula for computing likelihood ratios during sequential nanobody mutations
items.answer: A lot of that comes down to the fact that the AI agents decided they want to make a sequence of mutations. They start with some wild-type nanobody, which is basically an existing nanobody people tried before, but those nanobodies do not really work for recent variants of COVID. The agents take those as a starting point and then make sequential modifications by introducing mutations on top of that nanobody. A lot of the fine art in computing the likelihood score depends on how you measure the changes in the likelihood. Do you say, compared to the original wild type, how does the likelihood increase after every mutation you make? But what happens if you make the second mutation? Do you want to compare that with the first mutation, or do you compare that with the wild type? There are debates in the literature about how you want to approach that, with different approaches. The agents developed a specific formula for computing those likelihood ratios that, in my view, after the fact, is actually pretty reasonable.

items.question: How do you structure research in the Virtual Lab to mirror how your physical lab works?
items.object: The Virtual Lab’s research process
items.answer: The Virtual Lab has a set of AI agents: the AI professor, like a PI, and a bunch of AI experts with different domain expertise. There are basically two ways the Virtual Lab makes research progress. One is what we call group meetings, and the second is individual meetings. These are all designed to mirror how my physical lab here works at Stanford. In a group meeting, all the different AI agents come together. The AI professor would say, “Here's the meeting agenda,” maybe some questions we want to answer by the end of the meeting. Then all the agents go around the table and provide their thoughts on the meeting agenda and updates on their results, and in the end the professor takes the consensus and reaches some sort of solution with the entire team on the solutions to those questions.

items.question: How do you divide research work between group meetings and one-on-one meetings in the Virtual Lab?
items.object: Group meetings and one-on-one meetings in the Virtual Lab
items.answer: We use group meetings to try to decide some of the general directions of the research project, for example whether to design nanobodies or antibodies. That decision is made in one of these Virtual Lab group meetings. The second mode of research is what we call one-on-one meetings, where maybe the AI professor would say, “Now we need to write specific code, for example, to modify ESM, and the best agent for doing that is probably the computational biologist.” In that one-on-one meeting, the computational biologist meets with the professor agent. We also have a critic agent whose job is to provide constructive feedback to all of these meetings, and the goal of that one-on-one meeting is to solve each of the specific tasks.

items.question: How do you see the relationship between human guidance and the professor agent's autonomy in organizing a Virtual Lab project?
items.object: Human guidance and the professor agent's team selection in the Virtual Lab
items.answer: The human interaction comes from us mostly interacting with the professor agent. Essentially, at the start of the project, we tell the professor agent what we want to do, which could be a high-level description. We could say, “For this part, we want to design vaccines or therapeutics for SARS-CoV-2.” We could have picked different projects; we could have said we want to study quantum computers or climate, so it's a very versatile framework. Based on our high-level specifications, the professor agent would say, “Here are the kinds of relevant expertise that we would want to have on the team.” The professor creates and selects which team members to bring into the team. For the therapeutics project, the professor agent decided we want an immunologist agent, a computer science agent, and a computational biology agent. The professor's job is basically like recruiting the relevant members and selecting them to come on this quest. It depends on what the goal of the quest is; different members will get selected. The level of feedback that we provide to the professor tends to be this more high-level feedback.

items.question: Where do you think human expertise makes a difference in overseeing the Virtual Lab’s AI research agents?
items.object: Human expertise and oversight in the Virtual Lab
items.answer: I think where the expertise of the human is, is to also look over the shoulder of all these different agents and provide some constructive feedback to say that maybe here are some potential mistakes, or this doesn't look right. The nice thing about all these Virtual Labs is that all of their meetings, the group meetings and the one-on-one meetings, happen through natural language, so they all talk to each other through natural language. Basically, at the end of every meeting, the professor agent creates a summary, essentially meeting minutes, and presents that to us, the human researchers, so we can look over their meeting minutes. Sometimes we give feedback and say, “Did you think about this?” or “Did you think about that?” If we see that they're potentially going down a path that may be difficult to validate experimentally, then we can provide that feedback.

items.question: How do you assess the Virtual Lab paradigm's readiness for broader use by scientists?
items.object: The Virtual Lab paradigm and its readiness for broader scientific use
items.answer: We're very excited about this paradigm, but I also want to say that it's still relatively early stages. In the near future, we want to provide a V2 of this Virtual Lab that will be much easier for everybody to use, especially scientists from different domains who might not be familiar with coding or how to use these language models. Right now it's still a little bit bespoke because this is the first iteration and the first case study that we did, solving this nanobody design for SARS-CoV-2, but we do want to make it much more generalizable and easier to use in the future with some more interactive interfaces.

items.question: How do you compare the Virtual Lab agents' decision to pursue nanobodies with the surprising moves made by AlphaGo?
items.object: The Virtual Lab agents' choice of nanobodies compared with AlphaGo's surprising moves
items.answer: In terms of the surprisingness of this, compared to AlphaGo there's some interesting similarities and differences. In some sense it's not as surprising, perhaps, because the agents provide an explanation. In one of the early group meetings they said, “Nanobodies are known to be smaller, and they're easier to predict and easier to design.” That's relatively easy for us to understand. I'm not an expert in nanobodies, but I looked at that and said, “Okay, that seems like a reasonable decision.” That's why we didn't push back, whereas maybe some of the moves made by AlphaGo would have been difficult to explain even to experts. On the other hand, you can say that this decision made by the agents for nanobodies could be harder. With games like AlphaFold or AlphaGo, other games, it's a bit more controlled setting. You could self-play it out and see what the reward is at the very end; it's a deterministic reward. But for these open-ended scientific projects, the reason why it's much harder than games is that it's open-ended. Until you do the experimental validation, you don't really know what's going to work or not. There's no notion that you can self-play and see the real-world experiment, because that part is still not automated. There's also a lot more uncertainty. These decisions are very consequential and really affect the entire research direction, and we only get to do it once, at least for now. In that sense, it could potentially be a harder kind of decision to make.

items.question: What advantages do you see in the Virtual Lab's parallel agent meetings compared with human research meetings?
items.object: Parallel agent meetings in the Virtual Lab
items.answer: One nice thing about these virtual agents is that their meetings are much faster than meetings, right? In the time that we sit around and introduce each other and have coffee, they already had hundreds of meetings. The other nice thing is that the virtual agents don't get tired. What we do in the Virtual Lab is that every main decision is done through multiple meetings in parallel. Basically, every key decision that we want the agents to make, they run five meetings in parallel. They discuss the same topic five different times in parallel, and then reach some sort of consensus. It's interesting that different parallel meetings sometimes end up with different suggestions and different decisions. Similar to if you and I discuss something maybe two different days, we might end up with two different outcomes. But the nice thing is that we can do more inference compute, basically more parallel meetings, and explore more different paths of what could play out. Then the professor looks across the meeting logs of all these parallel meetings and says, “Here's the overall consensus and here's what we should do going forward.” In that sense, these meetings for the Virtual Lab are much faster and much more efficient than some of the physical meetings we can have.

items.question: How do you assess whether a human team would have arrived at similar nanobody designs and workflows to the Virtual Lab?
items.object: Virtual Lab nanobody designs compared with human-designed alternatives
items.answer: It's not really clear that the human team would have ended up with similar designs, the similar workflows, because these are very hard problems. For example, some of these recent variants, like the JN.1 variant of SARS-CoV-2, don't actually have a great binder, even though certainly a lot of people have been working on these things. It's a very important problem, but the Virtual Lab nanobodies show quite promising binding profiles. I do want to give the caveat that I think we need to do a lot more experimental testing to really validate these.

items.question: Where do you see the biggest cost in the Virtual Lab’s nanobody workflow?
items.object: Experimental validation in the Virtual Lab’s nanobody workflow
items.answer: Certainly the biggest cost is still the experimental validations. This is where we work very closely with our collaborators at the Chan Zuckerberg Biohub, who are experts in doing these protein affinity assays. So that's where there still needs to be a lot of human time involved.

items.question: How do you assess the potential for advances in AI and biotechnology to accelerate scientific discovery over the next 5 to 10 years?
items.object: The convergence of AI and biotechnology as a driver of scientific progress
items.answer: I think we're definitely in a very exciting time where there's an intersection of advances in AI, especially around agents and reasoning models, and also advances in biotechnology. We now have different, better ways of perturbing the cell, better ways of measurement. That convergence, that intersection, is extremely exciting. It's hard to know what will happen—100 years takes a long time to project—but I do think that even in the next 5 to 10 years there'll be a lot of really exciting problems that we can tackle.

items.answer: Initially we set it up to mirror my actual group meetings; you have the meetings and individual meetings just because that's how we know how to do things as human researchers. That sociology aspect could also be fascinating to follow.

items.question: How do you think the AI critic should handle disagreement in Virtual Lab meetings?
items.object: The AI critic’s politeness in Virtual Lab meetings
items.answer: One thing that's kind of interesting is that every meeting has a critic, an AI critic whose job is to provide constructive feedback to everything that's been said. Sometimes the different agents disagree with each other. Of course, being language models, they're very nice about it and very polite, and they have to somehow resolve their disagreement. One thing that's kind of interesting is that these language models, because of RLHF, tend to be overly polite, I think. Especially the critic agent, maybe we do want it to be a little bit harsher—not mean, but a bit more direct, and say, “Oh yeah, this is a bad idea.”

items.question: Why do you see interpreting protein language models as an exercise in scientific discovery?
items.object: Interpreting protein language models as scientific discovery
items.answer: With human models, we have a pretty good idea of how to interpret what concepts are learned by a GPT-style human language model. We know the concept, like Golden Gate Bridge; we can see other particular neurons in a transformer that correspond to the Golden Gate Bridge. But what's fascinating with the protein language model is that there are some concepts we know; maybe I know a particular kind of protein domain and can see if that shows up somewhere in that protein language model. But I would say most of the concepts are probably not known to us. We don't have a good description of what these concepts are. This is where I see interpretation of a protein language model not just as exercising mechanistic interpretability, but as a sort of exercise in scientific discovery. I think there's a gold mine of new concepts potentially learned by this protein language model training over evolutionary-scale data that do not actually have good human analogues.

items.question: Why do you think protein language models have learned concepts that humans haven't documented?
items.object: Protein language models learning concepts beyond human annotations
items.answer: I think especially in these more specialized domains like proteins or biology, there's a very clear limitation of what we have written down in words or descriptions. I look at all the protein databases: people have tried to annotate different concepts, but everybody recognizes that we're limited in what we have annotated. There are a lot of things that we just haven't annotated. I think, to your point, this is a really exciting opportunity where these protein language models, I think, have learned new concepts. They have filled in some of the gaps in our knowledge, and now it's our job to see: can we extract those out using techniques like SAEs?

items.question: How do you think about the scope of concepts that can be extracted from protein language models?
items.object: The conceptual scope of protein language models and the prospects for extracting more concepts
items.answer: In some ways, I think proteins are a more constrained space than the entirety of human language. With human language, there's so many things you can talk about outside of science. In all these other domains, it could be code or different images, so there's a lot of diversity of information. But if I look at only the language of proteins, in some ways it is a narrower domain. That being said, I think we're in some sense scratching the tip of the iceberg. Something we're actively working on now is applying these approaches to larger protein language models. For example, we're also applying that now to AlphaFold models, where there's more structural information and those models are larger. I think there are going to be additional concepts we'll be able to extract out from these different models.

items.question: How do you see large language models helping you interpret the concepts learned by protein language models?
items.object: Large language models for annotating and interpreting protein model concepts
items.answer: Some might be new concepts and some might be extensions of existing ones. This is where I think there's a convergence of different technologies. We found this is a good use case for a large language model. We used Claude to help us automatically annotate some of these new concepts by pulling relevant information from different databases and comparing what's known about the proteins versus what's being activated by each of these concepts. This is where there could be an interesting convergence of the two things we talked about: maybe you can imagine having a Virtual Lab of different expert agents that can help us interpret what's going on behind the hood of this large protein language model.

But if I forget about all the details of the AI and just look at the literature and ask how often new motifs are reported, I don't think it's that frequent.

items.question: What do you see as the main limitation to improving AI models for proteins, protein interactions, and small molecules?
items.object: Data limitations in AI models for proteins, protein interactions, and small molecules
items.answer: For certain domains of proteins, protein interactions, and small molecules, we're still data-limited rather than compute-limited. Even with AlphaFold 3 and the latest models, they still make mistakes on some of these disordered proteins or when looking at specific interaction domains. I expect those are the areas where we'll need to see a lot more data and more experimental data to validate and improve the models.

items.question: How do you view the move from studying individual proteins to studying cells and organs in AI for biology?
items.object: Moving from protein-level analysis to cells and organs in AI for biology
items.answer: I think a protein is not simple, but it's also a relatively self-contained unit of analysis. Ultimately, especially when it comes to human disease and human health, what we care about is really things at a larger scale level of cells and also organs. At that point, that's actually a bunch of other research projects we're doing in my group, so maybe we can have another discussion about those. I think that's also an area where there's been a lot of really exciting progress.
